INDIVIDUALIZED FAMILY SERVICE PLAN (IFSP) REVIEW
Programa Infantil y de Niños Pequeños de Carolina del Norte / North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program

1. INFORMACIÓN DE IDENTIFICACIÓN / IDENTIFYING INFORMATION

Child's Name: Mateo Alejandro Flores Ramírez ("Teo")
Date of Birth: March 3, 2024
Age at this review: 2;5
Gestational age at birth: 34 weeks
Birth weight: 4 lbs 2 oz
Apgar scores: 6 and 8
Primary caregivers: mother Lucía Ramírez Torres and father Alejandro Flores Medina
Sibling: Valentina Flores Ramírez, age 6;2
Address: 412 Hollyridge Lane, Durham, Durham County, NC 27704
Medicaid ID: DMA007741239C
CDSA Record ID: CDSA-00482
Primary languages in the home: Spanish and English (bilingüe)

2. OFICINA DEL CDSA Y COORDINACIÓN DE SERVICIOS / CDSA OFFICE AND SERVICE COORDINATION

La familia recibe servicios a través de la Agencia de Servicios para el Desarrollo Infantil del Condado de Durham (CDSA de Durham). This office, known in English as the Children's Developmental Services Agency, coordinates evaluation and service delivery for children birth to three under the North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program.

Service Coordinator: Brianna Walsh, employed by the Agencia de Servicios para el Desarrollo Infantil del Condado de Durham (CDSA de Durham)
Phone: (919) 555-0148
Email: bwalsh@cdsadurham.org

Ms. Walsh coordinó la reunión de revisión y estuvo presente junto con la madre, Lucía Ramírez Torres, y la terapeuta intérprete.

3. HISTORIA MÉDICA Y DE NACIMIENTO / BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Teo was born on March 3, 2024 at Duke Regional Hospital at 34 weeks gestation following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. He weighed 4 lbs 2 oz at birth with Apgar scores of 6 and 8. He was admitted to the Level III Neonatal Intensive Care Unit at Duke Regional Hospital for 19 days, where he received respiratory support and phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia.

Attending neonatologist in the NICU: Dr. Raj Patel
Discharge summary noted mild hypotonia, consistent with prematurity.

Current pediatrician: Dr. Susan Whitfield, MD
Lucía Ramírez Torres reportó que su hijo "siempre fue un bebé muy tranquilo, casi demasiado tranquilo," lo cual motivó la referencia temprana al CDSA.

Mateo was referred to the CDSA de Durham at 3 months of age due to prematurity risk factors. Initial IFSP was developed on June 10, 2024. Developmental evaluation at that time, administered by Camila Soto Jiménez, MS, CCC-SLP, showed delays in expressive communication.

No known allergies. Hearing screening passed bilaterally per newborn hearing screen on March 5, 2024. Vision screening within normal limits per pediatric visit on July 22, 2026.

4. INQUIETUDES Y PRIORIDADES DE LA FAMILIA / FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

Durante la entrevista, Lucía Ramírez Torres compartió, con la ayuda de la intérprete Rosa Elena Martínez: "Lo que más queremos es que Mateo pueda decirnos lo que necesita, que no se frustre tanto cuando no lo entendemos." She added, "At daycare, se pone a llorar porque no puede decir lo que quiere, and that breaks my heart."

El padre, Alejandro Flores Medina, agregó: "Queremos que hable en los dos idiomas, español e inglés, porque toda la familia habla español en casa pero en la guardería hablan inglés."

Priority 1: Mateo will use words or signs to request preferred items instead of crying or pulling.
Priority 2: Family wants strategies for supporting bilingual language development at home and in daycare.
Priority 3: Family wants support navigating services through WIC and understanding his continued eligibility through the CDSA de Durham.

5. RUTINAS DIARIAS / DAILY ROUTINES

Teo se despierta alrededor de las 7:00 a.m. y desayuna con su abuela, Rosa Torres, quien lo cuida tres días por semana mientras los padres trabajan. Mother works at Triangle Insurance Group and father works at Carolina Steel Fabrication.

On Tuesdays and Thursdays, Teo attends Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, where his classroom teacher is Ms. Hannah Dawkins. At daycare he plays alongside classmates including Sofía, with whom he has begun to share toys.

Por las tardes, Mateo juega con el perro de la familia, Max, en el patio trasero. Bath time is around 6:30 p.m., followed by books read in both languages, and bedtime by 8:00 p.m.. Los fines de semana, la familia a menudo visita a su primo Diego, hijo de la tía de Alejandro Flores Medina.

6. NIVELES ACTUALES DE DESARROLLO / PRESENT LEVELS OF DEVELOPMENT

Speech-language evaluation was completed by Camila Soto Jiménez, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual speech-language pathologist employed by Carolina Bilingual Therapy Partners, PLLC, with interpretation support from Rosa Elena Martínez.

Standardized assessment: Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), Spanish-English bilingual edition.
Auditory Comprehension standard score: 78 (7th percentile)
Expressive Communication standard score: 72 (3rd percentile)
Age equivalent range: 16-19 months
Confidence interval: 68-82

Articulation screening using the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) was not formally administered due to limited verbal output; informal stimulability testing was used instead.

Expressive vocabulary is estimated at 12-15 words in English and Spanish combined, with frequent use of gestures. During the session, Mateo requested water by producing "awa" for the target word "agua", achieving 3 of 5 trials with moderate cues. He attempted his sister's name, producing "Bale" in approximation of Valentina, which the family confirmed as his typical pronunciation.

Receptively, Teo followed one-step directions in Spanish 8/10 trials and in English 6/10 trials. He identified common objects by pointing with 90% accuracy across both languages.

Oral-motor exam was within functional limits. Phonemic inventory includes /m/, /p/, /b/, and emerging /t/; /k/ and /g/ are stimulable with minimal cues. Intervention approach incorporates principles of Hanen and responsive-interaction strategies, with emerging use of PROMPT tactile cueing for bilabial sounds.

Occupational therapy evaluation completed by Jennifer Patel, OTR/L noted mild fine motor delay consistent with gross motor findings from physical therapy evaluation completed by Michael Chen, PT, DPT, who documented gross motor skills at the 9th percentile on the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition (Bayley-4).

7. OTRAS AGENCIAS Y RECURSOS / OTHER AGENCIES AND RESOURCES

La familia participa en el programa de WIC del condado y recibe apoyo nutricional. También han sido referidos a Smart Start del Condado de Durham para servicios de cuidado infantil subsidiado. El Departamento de Servicios Sociales del Condado de Durham (DSS de Durham) fue contactado previamente para asistencia con Medicaid, proceso que fue completado exitosamente en April 2026.

8. RESULTADOS Y ESTRATEGIAS DEL IFSP / IFSP OUTCOMES AND STRATEGIES

Outcome 1: By the next review, Mateo will use 2-3 word combinations to request items and comment, in both English and Spanish, as measured by caregiver report and clinician observation during 3 of 4 consecutive sessions.
Strategies: Use of expansion and modeling in both languages; family coaching on "narrated play" during bath and mealtime routines; use of visual supports.

Outcome 2: Teo will increase his phonemic inventory to include /k/, /g/, and /f/ in spontaneous speech with moderate cues across home and daycare settings.
Strategies: PROMPT-informed tactile-kinesthetic cueing; coordination with daycare teacher Ms. Hannah Dawkins to reinforce target sounds during snack time.

Outcome 3: Family will report increased confidence supporting bilingual language development, as measured by a 1-point increase on the family-rated confidence scale at next review.
Strategies: Provision of bilingual handouts; monthly check-in calls between Camila Soto Jiménez, MS, CCC-SLP and Lucía Ramírez Torres; coordination with Brianna Walsh regarding continued eligibility.

9. HORARIO DE SESIONES / SESSION SCHEDULE

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monday | 9:00 a.m. | 9:45 a.m. | home - 412 Hollyridge Lane | Speech-Language Therapy | Camila Soto Jiménez, MS, CCC-SLP |
| Tuesday | 1:00 p.m. | 1:30 p.m. | Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, Durham | Occupational Therapy | Jennifer Patel, OTR/L |

INFORMACIÓN FAMILIAR

Teo vive con su madre, Guadalupe Ramírez Flores ("Lupita"), su padre, Jesús Soto Delgado ("Chuy"), y su hermana mayor, Sofía Soto Ramírez ("Sofi"), de 4 años. La familia vive en 482 Calle Roble, Graham, Condado de Alamance, NC 27253. Teléfono de la casa: (336) 555-0148. Correo electrónico de la madre: lupita.ramirezflores82@gmail.com.

La madre, Lupita, trabaja en la tienda Food Lion (Food Lion Store #2217) en el turno de la mañana. El padre, Chuy, trabaja en la planta empacadora de pollo Case Farms (en inglés, Case Farms Processing Plant), y también hace trabajos de fin de semana con una empresa constructora pequeña, Construcción Hermanos Reyes (Reyes Brothers Construction). La abuela materna, Carmen Flores Vega ("Nana Carmen"), cuida a Teo y a Sofi tres días a la semana mientras trabaja medio turno en el restaurante El Fogón Mexicano (en inglés, El Fogón Mexican Restaurant). El tío, José Ramírez ("Pepe"), ayuda económicamente a la familia y trabaja en la finca de los Hudson (en inglés, Hudson Family Farm) durante la temporada de cosecha. La tía, Rosa Ramírez, trabaja con un servicio de limpieza, Servicio de Limpieza Estrella (Star Cleaning Service).

La familia asiste a la Iglesia Bautista Nueva Esperanza y participa en el programa de cuentos bilingües de la Biblioteca Pública del Condado de Alamance los sábados por la mañana.

PREOCUPACIONES Y PRIORIDADES DE LA FAMILIA

En sus propias palabras, Lupita dijo: "Queremos que Teo pueda decirnos lo que necesita sin frustrarse, porque ahora llora o jala nuestra ropa. También nos preocupa que no lo entiendan bien en la guardería porque habla una mezcla de inglés y español." Chuy agregó: "Yo quiero que mi hijo juegue con otros niños y que ellos lo entiendan cuando habla."

RUTINAS DIARIAS

Teo se despierta alrededor de las 7:00 a.m. y desayuna con la familia. Asiste al Centro de Cuidado Infantil Little Angels de 8:30 a.m. a 3:00 p.m., donde su maestra, la Srta. Jennifer Alvarado, reporta que Teo juega cerca de otros niños, incluyendo a su compañero Josué, pero rara vez inicia el juego verbalmente. Por la tarde, la familia cena junta alrededor de las 6:30 p.m., y Teo participa en el baño y la rutina de dormir con su hermana Sofi, quien le canta canciones y le lee libros.

OTRAS AGENCIAS QUE USA LA FAMILIA

La familia recibe beneficios de WIC en la oficina del Condado de Alamance y fue referida a Smart Start del Condado de Alamance para servicios adicionales de apoyo familiar. También han tenido contacto con el Departamento de Servicios Sociales del Condado de Alamance (DSS) para asistencia con vivienda temporal durante el año pasado.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICA

Teo nació a las 32 semanas de gestación en el Hospital Regional Piedmont, con un peso de nacimiento de 1,580 gramos y puntuaciones de Apgar de 6 y 8. Pasó 18 días en la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Neonatales (UCIN) del Hospital Regional Piedmont bajo el cuidado del neonatólogo Dr. Roberto Hernández. Durante su estancia tuvo dificultades leves de alimentación y recibió terapia de succión-deglución con una especialista de la UCIN, Mónica Pérez. Su pediatra actual, la Dra. Sandra López, lo sigue para monitorear su desarrollo desde el alta hospitalaria. No se reportan otras hospitalizaciones, cirugías ni diagnósticos genéticos. La familia indica que Teo tuvo otitis media recurrente entre los 8 y 14 meses, tratada por la Dra. López sin necesidad de tubos de ventilación.

EVALUACIÓN DEL LENGUAJE Y HABLA

En la evaluación más reciente, Teo obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 76 (percentil 5) en el subtest de Comprensión Auditiva y 79 (percentil 8) en Comunicación Expresiva de la PLS-5 Spanish-English. Su intervalo de confianza fue 73-83. En producción espontánea, dijo "agua" y "mamá" de forma consistente, pero omitió consonantes finales, produciendo "ga" para "gato". Logró el fonema /k/ en posición inicial con claves mod en 7 de 10 ensayos. Su longitud media de enunciado (MLU) actual es de 2.4 palabras, comparado con 1.6 en la evaluación inicial.

El equipo, incluyendo a Lupita, Chuy, la coordinadora de servicios Ana Martínez y la patóloga del habla y lenguaje Patricia Gómez, acordó continuar los servicios de terapia del habla y lenguaje dos veces por semana en el hogar, con sesiones adicionales de consulta en el Centro de Cuidado Infantil Little Angels una vez al mes. La familia solicitó que las sesiones se mantengan en horario de 9:00 a.m. a 10:00 a.m. los martes y jueves, cuando Nana Carmen está disponible para recibir a la terapeuta si los padres están trabajando.

Buenas tardes, Patricia y Dr. Alvarado:

Adjunto, dentro de este mismo correo, el informe final de la evaluación de habla y lenguaje de Mateo ("Teo"), realizada en Piedmont Pediatric Therapy Partners, PLLC el September 15, 2026 y el September 22, 2026. Incluyo también el código de facturación y el diagnóstico sugerido para el expediente de Iredell County CDSA.

---

INFORME DE EVALUACIÓN DE HABLA Y LENGUAJE

Nombre del niño: Mateo Alejandro Ramírez Flores ("Teo")
Fecha de nacimiento: August 10, 2022
Edad cronológica en la evaluación: 4;2
Fecha(s) de evaluación: September 15, 2026, September 22, 2026
Fecha del informe: October 2, 2026
Evaluadora: Daniela Ortiz Vega, M.S., CCC-SLP, patóloga de habla-lenguaje bilingüe
Intérprete certificada presente en la segunda sesión: Marisol Tenorio
Expediente de la agencia: #IR-2026-00457
Número de Medicaid: NC48213967A
Médico de cabecera: Dr. Kevin Alvarado, Lake Norman Pediatric Clinic
Coordinadora de servicios: Patricia Gómez, Iredell County CDSA

RAZÓN DE LA REFERENCIA

Teo fue referido por su pediatra, el Dr. Kevin Alvarado de Lake Norman Pediatric Clinic, debido a preocupaciones sobre un retraso en el desarrollo del lenguaje expresivo y receptivo, así como dificultades de inteligibilidad del habla notadas tanto en casa como en la guardería. La madre, Lucía Flores, y el padre, Jorge Ramírez, reportan que Teo usa principalmente gestos y palabras sueltas para comunicarse, y que personas fuera del círculo familiar cercano frecuentemente no logran entenderlo.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y MÉDICA

Teo nació a las 34 semanas de gestación en Carolina Piedmont Health – Mooresville Campus, tras un embarazo complicado por preeclampsia materna. El peso al nacer fue de 4 libras 8 onzas y las puntuaciones de Apgar fueron de 7 al minuto y 9 a los cinco minutos. Teo permaneció en la unidad de cuidados intensivos neonatales (UCIN) de Carolina Piedmont Health – Mooresville Campus durante varias semanas por dificultad respiratoria leve e ictericia, sin necesidad de ventilación mecánica prolongada. Fue dado de alta con seguimiento por pediatría general.

A los 18 meses, el Dr. Alvarado notó que Teo no producía aún combinaciones de dos palabras y lo refirió a Iredell County CDSA para una evaluación de intervención temprana. En ese momento se estableció un Plan Individualizado de Servicios para la Familia (IFSP) con un resultado centrado en el lenguaje expresivo (Resultado 2 del IFSP: "Teo usará frases de dos a tres palabras para pedir y comentar"). Teo recibió servicios de intervención temprana en el hogar una vez por semana hasta cumplir los 3 años, cuando pasó al sistema escolar público para servicios de habla-lenguaje tipo preescolar especial.

La madre reporta antecedentes de infecciones recurrentes de oído medio: al menos cinco episodios de otitis media entre los 8 y los 24 meses de edad, tratados con antibióticos. Teo fue evaluado por otorrinolaringología y audiología en Blue Ridge ENT & Audiology por la Dra. Megan Sawyer y el audiólogo Dr. H. Patel, quienes colocaron tubos de ventilación bilaterales (timpanostomía) a los 26 meses de edad. Desde entonces no ha habido nuevos episodios de otitis, y una audiometría reciente en Blue Ridge ENT & Audiology mostró audición dentro de límites normales en ambos oídos.

No hay otros antecedentes médicos significativos. No usa anteojos. No tiene diagnóstico de trastorno del espectro autista, aunque la familia reporta que un primo paterno, Brandon Castillo, tiene diagnóstico de autismo y recibe servicios en su escuela.

HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y DE LENGUAJE

Teo vive con su madre, Lucía Esperanza Flores Hernández; su padre, Jorge Luis Ramírez Mejía; y su hermana mayor, Valentina Ramírez Flores, de 8 años, quien cursa tercer grado en Mooresville Intermediate School. La familia reside en 428 Birchwood Lane, Mooresville, 28115, en Iredell County.

La madre, Lucía Flores, trabaja dos empleos: por las mañanas limpia habitaciones en Lakeside Inn & Suites y por las noches trabaja en el turno nocturno de KPC, una planta procesadora cercana. El padre, Jorge Ramírez, trabaja como conductor de camión para Blue Ridge Trucking Co. y frecuentemente pasa varias noches fuera de casa por rutas largas. Debido a los horarios de ambos padres, la abuela materna, Rosa Elena Hernández Vargas, cuida a Teo y a Valentina la mayoría de las tardes después de la guardería, y una vecina, Noemí Castillo, los cuida algunos fines de semana cuando ambos padres trabajan turnos que coinciden.

La madre nació en el pueblo de El Rosario, Copán, Honduras, y emigró a los Estados Unidos a los 19 años. La abuela paterna de Teo todavía vive en El Rosario, Copán, Honduras, y la familia la visita cada par de años. El español es el idioma predominante en el hogar; los padres estiman que Teo escucha español aproximadamente el 70% del tiempo y inglés el 30% restante, principalmente a través de la guardería, la televisión y su hermana, quien es más dominante en inglés.

Teo asiste a Little Sprouts Daycare de lunes a viernes, donde su maestra, Ashley Thompson, reporta que es un niño cariñoso y sociable que juega bien en grupo pero que sus compañeros, como Josué Martínez y Kimberly Nguyen, a menudo no entienden lo que dice y recurren a la maestra para "traducir". Ashley Thompson también observa que Teo se frustra cuando no logra comunicarse y a veces recurre a empujar o gritar.

En casa, la familia tiene un perro llamado Toby, al que Teo adora. Durante la sesión de juego, Teo señaló la puerta y dijo espontáneamente "Toby afuera" al ver al perro salir al patio, lo cual ejemplifica su nivel actual de combinación de palabras.

Los hitos del desarrollo motor grueso y fino fueron reportados dentro de límites normales: caminó de forma independiente a los 14 meses y actualmente puede subir escaleras alternando pies, usar tijeras con supervisión y vestirse parcialmente solo. No hay preocupaciones en el área de alimentación; Teo come una dieta variada sin dificultades de masticación o deglución reportadas.

OBSERVACIONES CONDUCTUALES

Teo se mostró inicialmente tímido al inicio de la primera sesión, pero se familiarizó rápidamente con la evaluadora y con la intérprete, Marisol Tenorio, durante la segunda sesión. Mantuvo atención conjunta de forma consistente, siguió instrucciones de un paso con apoyo gestual y mostró buen contacto visual. El juego simbólico estuvo presente pero fue limitado principalmente a secuencias de una sola acción (alimentar a un muñeco, hacer "dormir" a un animal de peluche).

PRUEBAS ADMINISTRADAS Y RESULTADOS

Se administraron las siguientes pruebas estandarizadas, con normas en español cuando estuvieron disponibles, complementadas con muestras de lenguaje espontáneo y un examen del mecanismo oral motor.

1. Preschool Language Scale, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish)

Subprueba                      Puntuación estándar    Percentil         Edad equivalente
Comprensión Auditiva           73             percentil 4    2;9
Comunicación Expresiva         68             percentil 2    2;6
Puntuación Total del Lenguaje  70             percentil 2    (IC 95%: 65-75)

Ambos dominios se encuentran por debajo del rango promedio esperado para la edad cronológica de Teo (4;2), con un desempeño expresivo más débil que el receptivo.

2. Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA) – Subprueba de Morfosintaxis

En español, Teo obtuvo una puntuación que lo ubica en el rango de riesgo, con omisión frecuente de artículos y de concordancia de género y número (por ejemplo, dijo ""la perro"" en lugar de ""el perro""). En la versión en inglés de la subprueba, administrada de forma informal dado el uso limitado del inglés en el hogar, el desempeño fue consistente con un aprendiz emergente de ese idioma y no se interpretó como indicador adicional de trastorno.

3. Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)

Puntuación estándar: 77 (percentil 6)

Patrones observados: reducción de grupos consonánticos (por ejemplo, ""pato"" producido como "[pato]" se mantuvo correcto, pero ""azul"" se produjo como "[asu]"), frontalización de velares (sustitución de /k/ por [t], como en ""casa"" producido "[tasa]"), y procesos de simplificación silábica. Teo produjo correctamente el fonema /ɾ/ en posición intervocálica en 6 de 10 ensayos, mejorando a 8 de 10 con mod cues (modelo más énfasis acústico). En una muestra espontánea, al señalar al perro saliendo, dijo "Toby come", lo cual fue codificado para inteligibilidad en contexto conocido.

4. Muestra de lenguaje espontáneo e inteligibilidad

En una muestra de 50 enunciados grabados durante el juego, la inteligibilidad global para oyentes familiarizados con Teo fue del 55%; para oyentes no familiarizados (calculada por la evaluadora y la intérprete de forma independiente), la inteligibilidad descendió al 30%. La longitud media de enunciado en morfemas fue de 2.1, consistente con el nivel de combinación temprana de dos palabras, por debajo de lo esperado para la edad.

5. Examen del mecanismo oral-motor

Estructura y función oral-motora dentro de límites normales; sin indicios de apraxia del habla ni disartria. Frenillo lingual sin restricción funcional significativa.

6. Codificación SALT

Se utilizaron códigos [EW] para errores de palabra y [EO] para omisiones durante la transcripción de la muestra espontánea, siguiendo el protocolo estándar.

IMPRESIONES

Con base en los resultados obtenidos, Teo presenta un trastorno mixto de lenguaje receptivo-expresivo (más marcado en el dominio expresivo) y un trastorno fonológico, ambos consistentes a través de los dos idiomas del hogar, lo cual respalda un trastorno primario de lenguaje y no simplemente una diferencia esperada por bilingüismo normal en desarrollo. El historial de otitis media recurrente probablemente contribuyó, pero no explica por sí solo el patrón persistente observado después de la resolución de la pérdida auditiva conductiva. Los hallazgos son consistentes con los diagnósticos sugeridos F80.1 (trastorno del lenguaje expresivo) y F80.0 (trastorno fonológico).

El bajo nivel de inteligibilidad, especialmente con oyentes no familiarizados, representa una barrera funcional significativa para la participación de Teo en el entorno de guardería y, próximamente, en el entorno escolar. La frustración conductual reportada por Ashley Thompson y por los padres parece estar directamente relacionada con las limitaciones comunicativas, no con un trastorno conductual primario.

RECOMENDACIONES

1. Se recomienda terapia de habla-lenguaje individual, idealmente en español con apoyo en inglés, dos veces por semana, con revisión del IFSP y actualización del Resultado 2 para incluir metas de fonología e inteligibilidad además de las metas de longitud de enunciado.
2. Se recomienda el uso de estrategias de Hanen ("It Takes Two to Talk") para entrenar a los padres y a la abuela, Rosa Elena Hernández Vargas, en técnicas de expansión y de espera comunicativa durante las rutinas diarias.
3. Para el componente fonológico, se recomienda un enfoque de intervención tipo Cycles, dirigido a grupos consonánticos y a la sustitución de velares, con posible incorporación de apoyo táctil-kinestésico tipo PROMPT si el progreso con claves verbales es limitado.
4. Se recomienda coordinación con Iredell County CDSA para la transición oportuna de servicios de intervención temprana a servicios preescolares especiales antes de que Teo cumpla los 5 años.
5. Se recomienda que la familia continúe el seguimiento anual de audición con Blue Ridge ENT & Audiology dado el historial de otitis media.
6. Se recomienda compartir estrategias de apoyo con la maestra de guardería, Ashley Thompson, y considerar una breve consulta en el aula para modelar estrategias con los compañeros, incluyendo a Josué Martínez y Kimberly Nguyen.

CÓDIGOS DE FACTURACIÓN SUGERIDOS

96110 – Evaluación del desarrollo con instrumento estandarizado, cuando aplique para coordinación con pediatría.

CAROLINA BILINGUAL SPEECH & LANGUAGE SERVICES, PLLC
(d/b/a Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services; referred to below as "CBSLS")
Comprehensive Speech-Language Evaluation / Evaluación Integral del Habla y el Lenguaje

1. IDENTIFYING INFORMATION

Client: Mateo Alejandro Ramos Flores ("Mateo")
Date of Birth: March 14, 2021
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 4;7
Evaluation Dates: September 8, 2025 and September 15, 2025
Report Date: 09/22/2025
Medicaid ID: 987654321B
Record/Case ID: LD-24-00871
Parents/Guardians: Lucía Rodríguez Ramos (mother), Carlos Ramos Flores (father)
Home Address: 482 Willow Creek Lane, Raleigh, Wake County, NC 27610
Home Phone: (919) 555-0148
Mother's Email: lrodriguezramos25@gmail.com
Examining Clinician: Daniela Fuentes, M.S., CCC-SLP, Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist, Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC ("CBSLS")
Referral Source: Dr. Patricia Chen, pediatrician, via the Wake County CDSA (Children's Developmental Services Agency)
Service Coordinator: Brenda Whitfield, Wake County CDSA
Interpreter present second session: Jorge Santos, certified medical/educational Spanish interpreter

2. REASON FOR REFERRAL

Mateo was referred for a comprehensive speech-language evaluation by his pediatrician, Dr. Patricia Chen, after his mother, Lucía Rodríguez Ramos, expressed concern during a well-child visit on el martes 4 de junio de 2025 that Mateo "no habla tan claro como los demás niños de su edad" ("doesn't speak as clearly as other kids his age"). Mateo currently attends Little Sprouts Early Learning Center in Garner, where his lead teacher, Ms. Amanda Lopez, and assistant teacher, Sra. Carmen Torres, both reported difficulty understanding his speech, particularly in group settings. This evaluation was conducted under CPT codes 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression) and 92507 (individual treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder), the latter billed for a diagnostic therapy probe session.

3. BACKGROUND INFORMATION / ANTECEDENTES

3.1 Birth and Medical History

Mateo was born at 37 weeks gestational age 37 weeks at Blue Ridge Regional Medical Center in Raleigh on March 14, 2021, following a pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension. Birth weight was 5 lbs 6 oz and Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively. Mateo spent 11 days in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit at Blue Ridge Regional Medical Center under the care of neonatologist Dr. Robert Kim for mild respiratory distress and feeding difficulties requiring a nasogastric tube. Mother reports no known complications since NICU discharge. Mateo's pediatrician, Dr. Patricia Chen, has followed him since birth and noted during a visit on 01/09/2024 that his receptive and expressive language milestones appeared delayed relative to norms. An ENT evaluation with Dr. Michael Osei on November 3, 2024 ruled out hearing loss; tympanometry was within normal limits bilaterally, and Mateo passed a pure-tone screening at 20 dB HL across frequencies.

Mother reports no significant illnesses, no seizures, and no hospitalizations since the NICU stay. Mateo takes no current medications. Family medical history is notable for a maternal uncle with a reported "problema del habla" (speech problem) as a child, per report from Rosa Flores, Mateo's abuela (maternal grandmother), who lives with the family and assists with childcare three days a week.

3.2 Developmental History

Per parent report, Mateo sat independently at 6 months, walked independently at 14 months, and said his first words around 18 months, later than his older sister. Mother reports that single-word vocabulary did not expand meaningfully until around 26 months, and that two-word combinations did not emerge consistently until closer to 34 months. Lucía Rodríguez Ramos stated, "siempre entendía todo lo que le decíamos, pero no podía decirnos lo que quería" ("he always understood everything we told him, but he couldn't tell us what he wanted").

4. FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y LINGÜÍSTICA

Mateo lives at home with his mother, Lucía Rodríguez Ramos; his father, Carlos Ramos Flores; his older sister, Valentina Ramos, age 7, who attends second grade at Pinewood Elementary School; and his younger brother, Diego Ramos, age 1. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Flores, lives in the home and is a primary caregiver during the day, alongside an occasional babysitter, Esperanza Cruz, who watches Mateo and his siblings on weekend evenings.

The home language environment is bilingual. Lucía Rodríguez Ramos reports speaking primarily Spanish with the children, estimating approximately 70% Spanish and 30% English input at home. Carlos Ramos Flores speaks a mix of both languages, code-switching frequently, and reports, "yo le hablo en los dos, pero a veces se me sale todo en inglés en el trabajo" ("I speak to him in both, but sometimes it all comes out in English because of work"). Carlos Ramos Flores is employed at Southeastern Freight Lines, and Lucía Rodríguez Ramos works part-time at the Food Lion Distribution Center in Garner. Rosa Flores speaks exclusively Spanish with the children. At Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, instruction is delivered primarily in English, giving Mateo roughly 25-30 hours per week of English-dominant input outside the home.

Mother reports that Mateo mixes languages within sentences at home ("code-switching"), for example saying "quiero el ball" instead of "quiero la pelota." She does not view this as unusual, noting that his older sister, Valentina Ramos, did the same at a similar age and later became fully bilingual with age-appropriate skills in both languages.

The family receives support through Smart Start of Wake County for early childhood resources and has an open case with the Wake County CDSA for developmental services coordination, managed by Brenda Whitfield. The family was also connected with WIC services during Mateo's infancy.

At Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, Mateo's teachers, Ms. Amanda Lopez and Sra. Carmen Torres, report he is social and plays well with peers but is frequently misunderstood, especially by unfamiliar listeners. A classmate, Ethan Brooks, reportedly often says "I don't know what he's saying" during group play, according to Ms. Lopez. Mateo has one close friend at daycare, Sofía Nuñez, who mother reports "siempre le entiende, no sé cómo" ("always understands him, I don't know how").

The family has a pet dog. During the home observation portion of testing, Mateo pointed at the dog and said "Rocky kowwe" for "Rocky corre" (the dog runs), illustrating difficulty with the liquid /r/ sound in both languages.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES

The following standardized and informal measures were administered across two sessions, on 3 de marzo de 2025 (initial contact and intake) and the formal testing dates of September 8, 2025 and September 15, 2025, at the CBSLS clinic located at 1420 Falls Pointe Drive, Suite 220, Raleigh, NC 27609:

- Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), Spanish and English editions
- Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals Preschool-3 (CELF Preschool-3)
- Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)
- Bilingual English Spanish Assessment (BESA)
- Spontaneous language sample (English and Spanish contexts)
- Oral-motor examination
- Hearing screening review (records from Dr. Michael Osei)
- Parent interview and Hanen-informed caregiver questionnaire
- Clinical observation at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center on September 10, 2025 at 9:30 AM

Daniela Fuentes administered all measures. Jorge Santos interpreted for portions of the parent interview on September 15, 2025 when Carlos Ramos Flores was present, to ensure both parents could contribute fully in their preferred language.

6. TEST RESULTS / RESULTADOS DE LAS PRUEBAS

6.1 Standardized Testing Summary

Test / Subtest | Date Administered | Standard Score | 95% CI | Percentile
PLS-5 (English), Auditory Comprehension | 09/08/2025 | 76 | 70-82 | 5th
PLS-5 (English), Expressive Communication | 09/08/2025 | 68 | 61-75 | 2nd
BESA, Spanish Morphosyntax | 09/15/2025 | 79 | 73-85 | 8th
BESA, Spanish Phonology | 09/15/2025 | 81 | 74-88 | 10th
CELF Preschool-3, Core Language Score | 09/08/2025 | 71 | 65-77 | 3rd
GFTA-3, Standard Score | 09/15/2025 | 65 | 58-72 | 1st

Age equivalents derived from the PLS-5 Expressive Communication subscale fell within the 2;6–3;0 range, representing a gap of 19-25 months below Mateo's chronological age of 4;7.

6.2 Articulation and Phonology

On the GFTA-3, Mateo demonstrated the following sound errors, consistent across English and Spanish contexts: final consonant deletion of /s/, gliding of /l/ and /r/ to [w] (e.g., target "pelota" produced as "pewota"), and stopping of /f/ to [p]. During the spontaneous language sample, Mateo produced the target word "sopa" as "topa," and "flor" as "pol." Intelligibility to an unfamiliar listener was judged to be approximately 40% in connected speech.

On a 10-trial probe of word-initial /k/ production with mod cues, Mateo achieved 8/10 (80%) accuracy, suggesting stimulability for this sound with support. On a comparable probe for /r/, he achieved 3 of 5 trials correct with max cues, indicating this sound remains significantly more difficult.

6.3 Language Sample Analysis

A 50-utterance spontaneous language sample was coded using SALT conventions. Mean length of utterance (MLU) in English was 2.8 morphemes, and in Spanish was 3.1 morphemes, both below age expectations. Several utterances were coded [EW] for word-finding difficulty, and Mateo frequently relied on gesture to supplement verbal output when a target word was not accessible.

7. CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS / IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Mateo presents with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder affecting both English and Spanish, alongside a moderate-to-severe speech sound disorder affecting intelligibility in both languages. His difficulties are not attributable to his bilingual environment; weaknesses were documented across both English and Spanish measures using instruments normed for bilingual populations (BESA), ruling out typical second-language acquisition patterns or normal cross-linguistic transfer as the sole explanation.

Mateo's pattern of errors—gliding of liquids, final consonant deletion, and reduced intelligibility across both languages—along with below-average scores in both receptive and expressive language domains in both languages, is consistent with a true bilingual language impairment rather than a language difference. Hearing has been ruled out as a contributing factor per Dr. Michael Osei's records. Oral-motor structure and function were within normal limits, with no evidence of dysarthria or significant oral-motor weakness; findings are inconsistent with childhood apraxia of speech, though mild groping behaviors were noted on a small number of multisyllabic word attempts and should continue to be monitored.

8. DIAGNOSTIC IMPRESSION

Based on the results of this evaluation, Mateo meets diagnostic criteria for:

- F80.2 — Mixed Receptive-Expressive Language Disorder
- F80.0 — Phonological Disorder (Speech Sound Disorder)

These diagnoses are supported by standardized testing at or below the 10th percentile across multiple domains in both of Mateo's languages, parent and teacher report of functional communication difficulty, and direct clinical observation.

9. RECOMMENDATIONS / RECOMENDACIONES

9.1 It is recommended that Mateo receive individual speech-language therapy twice weekly, 30 minutes per session, billed under CPT code 92507, targeting:
- Expansion of expressive vocabulary and syntax in both English and Spanish
- Remediation of /r/, /l/, /f/, and final consonant production in both languages
- Narrative and sequencing skills to support preliteracy development
- Continued monitoring for oral-motor planning difficulties

9.2 CBSLS recommends bilingual service delivery, with therapy conducted in both English and Spanish, consistent with the family's home language environment and best practice for bilingual language disorder intervention. Daniela Fuentes is available to continue as the treating clinician given her bilingual certification.

9.3 It is recommended that the Wake County CDSA, through service coordinator Brenda Whitfield, update Mateo's IFSP to reflect new outcome Outcome 3: improving expressive and receptive language skills in both English and Spanish across home and daycare settings, with a review date of March 2026.

9.4 Staff at Little Sprouts Early Learning Center, including Ms. Amanda Lopez and Sra. Carmen Torres, should be provided with strategies to support intelligibility, including requesting repetition, modeling target words, and allowing extra response time.

9.5 Family is encouraged to continue rich language exposure in both English and Spanish at home; current bilingual exposure should be maintained, not reduced, as bilingualism is not contributing to Mateo's disorder.

9.6 Re-evaluation is recommended in approximately 12 months, or sooner if progress plateaus, tentatively scheduled for the week of September 14, 2026.

9.7 A copy of this report should be forwarded to Dr. Patricia Chen's office and to the Wake County CDSA file for Mateo, Record ID LD-24-00871, Medicaid ID 987654321B.

10. SIGNATURES

This report was prepared by Daniela Fuentes, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist, on behalf of Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC (CBSLS), 1420 Falls Pointe Drive, Suite 220, Raleigh, NC 27609. Questions regarding this report may be directed to CBSLS at (919) 555-0177 or dfuentes@carolinabilingualslp.com.

___________________________
Daniela Fuentes, M.S., CCC-SLP
Carolina Bilingual Speech & Language Services, PLLC

Report completed: 09/22/2025
Distribution: Family; Dr. Patricia Chen; Wake County CDSA; Little Sprouts Early Learning Center (with parental consent)

PIEDMONT PEDIATRIC SPEECH & LANGUAGE SERVICES, PLLC
4521 Yanceyville Street, Greensboro, NC 27405

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Child's Name: María José Fuentes Rivas ("Majo")
Date of Birth: July 2, 2022          Chronological Age at Evaluation: 4;2
Date of Evaluation: September 18, 2026
Date of Report: September 25, 2026
CDSA Case ID: NC-CDSA-48217
Medicaid ID: 9284716503B
Home Language(s): Spanish (primary), English (secondary, from school exposure)
Referred By: Dr. Patricia Nguyen, Lakeside Pediatrics
Service Coordinator: Monica Alvarez, Piedmont Regional CDSA
Evaluator: Rebecca Chen, MS, CCC-SLP, Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Interpreter: Mr. Tom, Spanish Language Interpreter, present for the full session
Report Distribution: Eduardo Fuentes Castillo and Alejandra Rivas Morales (parents), Piedmont Regional CDSA, Lakeside Pediatrics

REASON FOR REFERRAL

María José Fuentes Rivas, known to her family as "Majo," is a 4;2-year-old girl referred by her pediatrician, Dr. Patricia Nguyen of Lakeside Pediatrics, for a comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation. Concerns include limited intelligibility in both Spanish and English, short and simplified sentence structure, and difficulty following multi-step directions at home and in her Pre-K classroom. Her mother, Alejandra Rivas Morales, and her father, Eduardo Fuentes Castillo, both report that María José is often frustrated when she cannot make herself understood, and that her older brother, Diego Fuentes Rivas, frequently speaks for her. This evaluation was requested to determine eligibility for continued early intervention services and to guide the transition planning conference with Guilford County Schools.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

María José lives with her parents, Eduardo Fuentes Castillo and Alejandra Rivas Morales, her older brother Diego Fuentes Rivas (7 years old), and her baby sister Camila Fuentes Rivas (10 months). The family home is located in Burlington, 27217, and the family also spends significant time at the home of María José's maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, who provides after-school care for the children several days a week while the parents work.

Alejandra Rivas Morales works nights at Carolina Poultry Processing Plant, where she has been a line supervisor for three years. In Spanish, the family refers to her workplace as la Procesadora de Pollo Carolina, the plant located near the edge of town. Eduardo Fuentes Castillo works days as a framing crew lead for Triad Construction Company; at home, his wife and his mother describe his job as trabaja para la Constructora Triad, levantando casas nuevas. Because both parents' schedules overlap on weeknights, doña Lupe picks the children up from daycare and school and stays with them until one parent returns.

Other members of the extended family contribute to childcare and household support. María José's aunt, su tía Rosa, works as a server at El Fogón Mexican Restaurant; the family also calls it el Restaurante El Fogón when speaking Spanish at home. An uncle, su tío Manuel, works at Sunrise Dairy Farm, known in Spanish as la Granja Sunrise, where he milks and feeds the herd before dawn. A cousin, su prima Marisol, works part time at Value Mart General Store, referred to by the family as la Tienda Value Mart. Doña Lupe herself works several mornings a week for Bright Homes Cleaning Service, which the family calls el Servicio de Limpieza Bright Homes, before she begins her afternoon childcare duties.

The family keeps a small dog, Rocky, who is often present during home visits and appears to motivate María José's spontaneous verbalizations; during the evaluation, she pointed at the family's photo of the dog and said "Rocky run" when asked what was happening in the picture.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

María José was born at 38 weeks gestation at Cone Health Women's Hospital via scheduled cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 6 lbs 11 oz and Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes respectively. The pregnancy was reportedly uncomplicated apart from mild gestational hypertension managed with monitoring. María José was discharged home at 2 days of life with no NICU admission.

Developmental milestones were within normal limits for gross and fine motor domains: she walked independently at 13 months and fed herself with a spoon by 18 months. Parents report first words in Spanish ("mamá," "agua," "papá") emerged around 14 months, consistent with typical ranges, but word combinations were delayed, not appearing reliably until approximately 30 months. María José passed her newborn hearing screening and a repeat audiological screening at 3 years through Piedmont Regional CDSA, with results within normal limits bilaterally. There is no history of chronic otitis media, though she had two documented episodes of acute otitis media, both resolved with antibiotic treatment, at ages 2;1 and 2;8. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable; she takes no routine medications and has no known allergies. Her pediatrician, Dr. Patricia Nguyen, continues to monitor her growth and development at Lakeside Pediatrics.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

María José has been raised in a Spanish-dominant household since birth. Alejandra Rivas Morales reports that Spanish is used almost exclusively at home, including by doña Lupe, tía Rosa, and tío Manuel during visits. Diego Fuentes Rivas, who is bilingual from his own schooling, sometimes code-switches with his sister, and María José has begun to imitate short English phrases she hears from him and from television.

María José began attending Little Stars Daycare Center at 18 months, where exposure to English began informally through songs and routines. At age 3, she transitioned to the NC Pre-K program at Eastside Elementary School, part of Guilford County Schools, where she is now enrolled in la maestra Carmen's classroom with support from the assistant teacher, Miss Ana. Both educators report that María José participates eagerly in group activities but is difficult to understand in both languages, and that she sometimes watches a classmate, Sofia, before attempting a task herself, suggesting reliance on visual modeling. The family also briefly attended a parent-child playgroup through Smart Start of Guilford County when María José was 2 years old, which first raised concerns about her limited vocabulary relative to same-age peers.

Per parent and teacher report, María José's receptive skills are stronger in Spanish than in English, while her expressive output is reduced in both languages relative to expectations for her age. She has received early intervention speech-language services through Piedmont Regional CDSA since January 2025, with sessions delivered in the home by a bilingual provider, and has also received monthly consultative visits from an occupational therapist, Grace Kim, and a physical therapist, James Whitfield, though gross and fine motor skills are not current areas of concern.

EDUCATIONAL AND IFSP HISTORY

María José's current Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP) was last reviewed on March 12, 2026, at a meeting attended by both parents, doña Lupe, Monica Alvarez of Piedmont Regional CDSA, and the early intervention speech-language provider. The table below summarizes progress on each current IFSP outcome as of that review.

Outcome	Strategies	Progress	Date
Outcome 1: María José will use 3-word phrases in Spanish to request desired items across settings	Modeling, expansion, wait time, visual choice boards used by parents and doña Lupe	Met in home setting; emerging in classroom per la maestra Carmen	March 12, 2026
Outcome 2: María José will follow 2-step directions in Spanish without visual cues	Hand-over-hand fading, repetition, chunking of directions into smaller units	Partially met; consistent at home, inconsistent at Eastside Elementary School	March 12, 2026
Outcome 3: María José will produce age-appropriate consonant sounds in word-initial position	Articulation drills, auditory bombardment, minimal pairs with /k/ and /g/	Limited progress; continues to substitute [t] for /k/	March 12, 2026
Outcome 4: María José will increase mean length of utterance in English during classroom routines	Bilingual modeling by Miss Ana, peer modeling with Sofia, repeated songs and routines	Not yet met; English utterances remain primarily single-word	March 12, 2026

BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

The evaluation took place at the family home in Burlington on September 18, 2026, from 9:30 a.m. to 11:15 a.m., with Mr. Tom interpreting throughout. María José separated easily from her mother, Alejandra Rivas Morales, and engaged readily with toys and picture books. She demonstrated adequate attention for structured tasks of approximately 10 minutes before requiring a break, and transitioned appropriately between activities with minimal cueing. Eye contact and joint attention were age-appropriate. María José communicated primarily through single words and gestures in Spanish, occasionally combining two words ("más agua," "no quiero"), and used English only for a handful of memorized phrases ("bye bye," "all done"). Her mother and doña Lupe, who was also present for part of the session, confirmed that this sample was representative of her typical communication.

ASSESSMENT RESULTS

Standardized assessment was conducted in both Spanish and English using culturally and linguistically appropriate bilingual measures. Given María José's dual language exposure, scores are reported for both languages where applicable, and conceptual scoring was used on measures that support it.

Test / Subtest	Standard Score	Percentile	Range
Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA) Morphosyntax (Spanish)	79	8th	73-85
BESA Morphosyntax (English)	70	2nd	64-76
BESA Semantics (Conceptual Score)	76	5th	69-83
Preschool Language Scale-5 (PLS-5) Spanish Auditory Comprehension	82	12th	73-83
PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication	71	3rd	63-79
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3) Sounds-in-Words	68	2nd	61-75

On the BESA Morphosyntax subtest, María José obtained a Spanish standard score of 79 (8th percentile) and an English standard score of 70 (2nd percentile), both falling below average limits and consistent with a language disorder affecting both languages rather than a difference attributable solely to bilingual acquisition. On the Semantics subtest, conceptual scoring (crediting correct responses in either language) yielded a standard score of 76 (5th percentile), still below the average range.

On the PLS-5 Spanish form, María José's Auditory Comprehension standard score of 82 fell within the low average to below average range (12th percentile), while her Expressive Communication standard score of 71 fell well below average (3rd percentile), indicating a significant gap between what she understands and what she can express, even in her dominant language.

Articulation was assessed using the GFTA-3 in Spanish, with results interpreted alongside informal English sampling. María José obtained a standard score of 68 (2nd percentile), reflecting multiple sound errors beyond what would be expected for typical bilingual development at 4;2. Specific error patterns included consistent fronting of velar sounds, substituting [t] for /k/ and [d] for /g/ (e.g., "tasa" for "casa," "dato" for "gato"), as well as final consonant deletion in both languages (e.g., "pa" for "pan"). Liquid sounds were also inconsistent, with gliding observed for /ɾ/ (e.g., "paja" for "para"). Given her age, trilled and tapped Spanish rhotics are still developing, but the pattern of errors across multiple sound classes, combined with reduced intelligibility, is of clinical concern.

Oral mechanism examination revealed age-appropriate structure and function, with adequate labial, lingual, and velopharyngeal movement for speech. No evidence of dysarthria or apraxia characteristics (such as inconsistent errors on repeated productions or significant groping behaviors) was observed, though a brief trial of diadochokinetic tasks will be repeated at the next session to rule out subtle motor planning involvement.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE AND PRAGMATICS

A spontaneous language sample was collected during play-based interaction, coded using SALT conventions. María José's mean length of utterance in Spanish was 2.1 morphemes, below expectations for her age. Utterance types included frequent omissions, coded as [EW] for omitted words in several utterances (e.g., "quiero [EW] agua" for "quiero más agua"). She used primarily noun-verb or noun-noun combinations and demonstrated limited use of grammatical morphemes such as articles and plural markers in both languages.

Pragmatically, María José initiated communication appropriately, used gestures to supplement limited verbal output, and responded to her name consistently. She demonstrated turn-taking during simple games and sought adult attention when frustrated, often pulling on her mother's sleeve and vocalizing rather than using words. No concerns were noted regarding social reciprocity, restricted interests, or repetitive behaviors.

SUMMARY AND CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

María José Fuentes Rivas is a 4;2-year-old bilingual Spanish-English speaking girl who presents with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder affecting both of her languages, alongside a speech sound disorder characterized by fronting, final consonant deletion, and liquid simplification patterns beyond what is expected for typical bilingual development. Her difficulties are not attributable solely to normal second-language acquisition, as deficits are present in Spanish, her dominant and home language, as well as in English. The combination of reduced intelligibility, limited utterance length, and gaps between comprehension and expression is consistent with findings reported by her family, doña Lupe, and her teachers, la maestra Carmen and Miss Ana, at Eastside Elementary School.

Diagnostic impressions: Mixed Receptive-Expressive Language Disorder (ICD-10 F80.2) and Phonological Disorder (ICD-10 F80.0). These findings support continued eligibility for speech-language intervention services under Piedmont Regional CDSA and warrant consideration for continued services through Guilford County Schools at the time of her transition from Part C to Part B services.

Services provided during this evaluation are billed under CPT 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression) and CPT 96125 (standardized cognitive performance testing, interpretation and report).

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. María José should continue to receive individual speech-language therapy services at a frequency of at least twice weekly, delivered by a bilingual provider, with sessions split between Spanish-language goals and bilingual carryover strategies, as supported by Piedmont Regional CDSA.

2. Therapy should target phonological processes using a cycles-based approach (Cycles) to address fronting, final consonant deletion, and liquid simplification across both languages, with priority given to functional, highly used words first.

3. Expressive language goals should target increased utterance length and use of grammatical morphemes in Spanish, using strategies consistent with Hanen "It Takes Two to Talk" principles, which the family and doña Lupe can be coached to use during daily routines.

4. The family should be connected with bilingual home-practice materials, and parent coaching should include both Alejandra Rivas Morales and Eduardo Fuentes Castillo, as well as doña Lupe, given her significant caregiving role, so that strategies remain consistent despite varied work schedules at Carolina Poultry Processing Plant and Triad Construction Company.

5. Coordination is recommended between Piedmont Regional CDSA, Guilford County Schools, and the family to plan for a smooth transition from IFSP to IEP services prior to María José's entry into kindergarten, including a transition conference with la maestra Carmen and school-based evaluation staff.

6. Within the classroom at Eastside Elementary School, la maestra Carmen and Miss Ana are encouraged to continue bilingual modeling, pairing new English vocabulary with Spanish equivalents, and to use peer modeling opportunities such as pairing María José with classmates like Sofia during structured activities.

7. A follow-up audiological evaluation is recommended within the next year given her history of recurrent otitis media, to be coordinated through Lakeside Pediatrics with Dr. Patricia Nguyen.

8. Re-evaluation of speech and language skills is recommended in approximately 6 months, or sooner if significant changes in progress are observed, to update IFSP outcomes and inform transition planning.

This report reflects María José's performance on the date of testing and should be considered alongside ongoing clinical observation, parent report, and teacher input. Please contact this office with any questions.

Respectfully submitted,

Rebecca Chen, MS, CCC-SLP
Bilingual Speech-Language Pathologist
Piedmont Pediatric Speech & Language Services, PLLC
(336) 555-0142 | rchen@piedmontpedsslp.com

Foothills Speech & Language Services, PLLC

Speech-Language Evaluation Report

Date of Report: October 2, 2026
Dates of Evaluation: August 12, 2026 and August 19, 2026
Child's Name: Jesús Alejandro del Río ("Chuy")
Date of Birth: January 4, 2023
Chronological Age at Evaluation: 3;8
Parents/Guardians: Jorge del Río and Lucía Fernández-Ramos
Primary Language(s): Spanish and English
Interpreter Present: Alicia Vargas, certified medical interpreter
Referral Source: Dr. Hannah Osei, Blue Ridge Pediatrics at Falls Creek
Service Coordinator: David Whitfield, Western Piedmont Children's Developmental Services Agency (CDSA)
Medicaid ID: 882147563B
CDSA Case ID: CDSA-1182940
Evaluating Clinician: Rachel A. Boyd, M.S., CCC-SLP, NC License No. SLP-04827

Dear Mr. del Río and Ms. Fernández-Ramos,

Thank you for bringing Chuy in to see me on August 12, 2026 and again on August 19, 2026. It was a pleasure to meet your whole family and to hear more about how Chuy talks, plays, and learns at home. I know it can feel like a lot to sit through a long evaluation, so I want to start by saying how proud you should be of how hard Chuy worked both days, and how much he enjoyed the puppets and the bubbles we used to keep him engaged. This letter explains what we found, what it means, and what I recommend next. I have tried to write it in plain language, but if anything is confusing, please call me at (828) 555-0147 or email me at rboyd@foothillsspeech.com, and we can go over it together, with Ms. Vargas interpreting if that is easier for you.

Reason for Referral

Chuy was referred for this evaluation by his pediatrician, Dr. Hannah Osei, at Blue Ridge Pediatrics at Falls Creek, after his three-year well-child visit. You shared with Dr. Osei that Chuy was still hard to understand, even for family members, and that he was not yet combining words the way his older sister and brother did at his age. Dr. Osei referred your family to the Western Piedmont CDSA, where Mr. Whitfield completed an intake and arranged for this speech-language evaluation as part of Chuy's ongoing Individualized Family Service Plan, or IFSP. You told me the main things you hope to see change are that Chuy can ask for what he wants without getting frustrated, and that his teacher at daycare can understand him better during group time.

Background and Developmental History

Chuy lives at home with both of you, his sister Guadalupe "Lupita" del Río, who is six, and his brother José "Pepe" del Río, who is nine. His grandmother, Carmen del Río, lives nearby and watches him some afternoons while Ms. Fernández-Ramos is at work. You also mentioned that his cousin, Teodoro "Teo" Martínez, sometimes stays over on weekends and that Chuy has started copying some of Teo's English phrases, which has been both funny and a little confusing for everyone. The family dog, Rocky, is also a favorite of Chuy's, and several of his clearest words so far have been attempts at Rocky's name.

Chuy attends Little Sprouts Daycare three days a week, where his classroom teacher, Ms. Diane Lopez, has noted that he plays alongside peers but rarely initiates conversation. One peer in particular, Juan "Juanito" Castillo, has become a close play partner, and Ms. Lopez reports that Chuy will often point and gesture to Juanito rather than using words during free play. Little Sprouts Daycare partners with the county's Early Head Start program, and Chuy's classroom slot is subsidized through that partnership.

You described Chuy as an affectionate, social child who loves trucks, bubbles, and being outside. He sleeps well, eats a wide variety of foods, and has no significant behavioral concerns. He understands routines and follows simple directions at home when they are paired with gestures, but struggles more with directions that are spoken without visual support, especially in a noisy room.

Birth and Medical History

Chuy was born at 29 weeks gestation, weighing 2 lb 10 oz, following a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. He was delivered at Blue Ridge Health – Falls Creek Campus and spent 41 days in the Falls Creek Campus NICU. His Apgar scores were 6 and 8 at one and five minutes. During his NICU stay, he required supplemental oxygen for the first two weeks and had a brief course of phototherapy for jaundice. He was discharged home on monitors for two months, which were eventually weaned without incident.

Because of his prematurity, Chuy has had several follow-up visits with specialists. He was seen at Falls Creek Ear, Nose & Throat and Audiology Associates for recurrent ear infections, and underwent bilateral myringotomy with tube placement, CPT code 69436, at age 18 months under the care of Dr. Marcus Tran. A follow-up audiogram with Dr. Priya Nair, Au.D., at the same practice confirmed normal hearing sensitivity bilaterally as of June 3, 2026, with no further middle-ear effusion noted. You mentioned that the tubes have made a noticeable difference in how often Chuy responds to his name being called.

Chuy has no known allergies and takes no daily medications. He is up to date on his immunizations per Dr. Osei's records. There is no family history of autism, intellectual disability, or genetic syndromes reported, though you noted that Mr. del Río's brother was "a late talker" who caught up by school age.

Family and Language History

Your household is bilingual, with Spanish spoken predominantly at home and English introduced gradually through Little Sprouts Daycare and through Chuy's siblings, who are both English-dominant after starting school. You estimate that Chuy hears roughly seventy percent Spanish and thirty percent English in a typical week, though that balance shifts toward more English on the days he is in daycare.

Lupita and Pepe both met their early language milestones without concern, which is part of why Chuy's slower progress stood out to you. Ms. Fernández-Ramos works night shifts at Carolina Textile Mills, and Mr. del Río works days at Falls Creek Furniture Company, so childcare is shared among the two of you, Carmen del Río, and occasionally Teo. You reported that your family has received support from several community programs during Chuy's early years, including the Caldwell County WIC Program for nutrition support when he was an infant, Caldwell County Smart Start for a developmental screening at age two, and the Caldwell County Department of Social Services for help with childcare subsidies. Mr. Whitfield at the CDSA has coordinated Chuy's services since his initial IFSP was written, and you have found him responsive and easy to reach.

You estimate that Chuy currently uses between twenty and thirty understandable words across both languages, including a mix of Spanish and English forms such as "agua," "more," "mamá," and "up." He does not yet combine two words together consistently, and his sentence structure is essentially single-word at this stage. You have not noticed a strong preference for one language over the other, though you feel his Spanish vocabulary is slightly larger than his English vocabulary, which makes sense given how much more Spanish he hears at home.

Assessment Procedures

Over the course of two sessions, I administered a combination of standardized and informal measures, with portions presented in Spanish and portions in English, using Ms. Vargas to support administration and to help interpret Chuy's spontaneous Spanish utterances. Measures included the Preschool Language Scale-5 (PLS-5) Spanish edition, the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation-3 (GFTA-3), an oral-motor examination, a hearing screening consistent with current documented results, and a language sample collected during structured and unstructured play. Chuy was cooperative throughout both sessions, though he required frequent breaks and brief movement activities to stay engaged, particularly during the second session.

Billing for this evaluation was submitted under CPT code 92523 (evaluation of speech sound production with evaluation of language comprehension and expression).

Test Results

The table below summarizes Chuy's scores on formal testing. A standard score between 85 and 115 is considered within the broadly average range; scores below 78 generally fall more than one and a half standard deviations below the mean.

| Test / Subtest | Date Given | Standard Score | 95% Confidence Interval | Percentile Rank | Age Equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | 08/12/2026 | 76 | 68-84 | 5th | 2;3-2;6 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 08/12/2026 | 81 | 73-89 | 10th | 2;6-2;9 |
| PLS-5 Total Language Score | 08/12/2026 | 77 | 70-84 | 6th | 2;6–3;0 |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | 08/19/2026 | 72 | 64-80 | 3rd | 2;9-3;0 |

On the PLS-5, Chuy's scores in both auditory comprehension and expressive communication fell in the moderately to severely delayed range relative to same-age peers, with his understanding of language slightly weaker than his expression of it, which can be unusual and is worth watching. On the GFTA-3, his score reflects difficulty producing a wide range of consonant sounds, including final consonant deletion and cluster reduction patterns typical of younger children. Because Chuy is being raised bilingually, I interpreted these scores cautiously alongside the informal Spanish language sample described below, rather than relying on the English-normed scores alone.

Articulation and Phonology

During single-word and connected-speech sampling, Chuy demonstrated the following error patterns in both languages. He substitutes /t/ for /k/ in word-initial position, as in "tasa" for "casa." He deletes final consonants, producing "ma" for "más" and "do" for "dos." He reduces consonant clusters, saying "pato" for "plato." He also substitutes /g/ for the tapped /ɾ/ in medial position, producing "paga" for "para." In English, similar patterns were observed, including "tar" for "car" and "boo" for "boot." His intelligibility was estimated at approximately 30% to unfamiliar listeners and 60% to familiar listeners when context was known, which is consistent with what you have described at home.

When Ms. Boyd modeled a two-word carrier phrase and asked Chuy to imitate it using the family dog's name, he said "Rocky run" clearly and with appropriate rhythm, though he dropped the phrase into a single rushed unit rather than two distinct words, which illustrates the kind of morpheme omission noted throughout both sessions. With moderate cues, he was able to imitate 3 of 5 target two-word combinations, such as "more agua" and "up please," though spontaneous use of these same combinations during play was limited to 1 of 10 opportunities.

Oral-Motor and Hearing Status

Oral-motor examination revealed structures and function within normal limits for speech, with adequate lip rounding, tongue elevation, and jaw stability observed during both speech and feeding tasks reported by you. Given Chuy's documented hearing within normal limits as of June 3, 2026, per Dr. Nair's audiogram, hearing loss does not appear to be contributing to his current speech and language profile, though I recommend continued monitoring given his history of chronic ear infections prior to tube placement.

Receptive and Expressive Language Sample

During a fifteen-minute play-based language sample, Chuy produced 22 intelligible single-word utterances and 4 two-word combinations across both languages. His mean length of utterance was approximately 1.2 morphemes, which falls well below expectations for his chronological age of 3;8. He used gestures, including pointing and pulling your hand, to request items in approximately 40% of observed communicative attempts, suggesting that gesture remains a primary communication strategy rather than a supplement to verbal language. He demonstrated appropriate joint attention, turn-taking, and eye contact throughout both sessions, and showed no repetitive behaviors or unusual play patterns that would raise concern for a broader developmental or social-communication difference.

Clinical Impressions

Based on today's results, parent and teacher report, and Chuy's developmental and medical history, he presents with a moderate expressive and mild-to-moderate receptive language delay, along with a moderate speech sound disorder affecting intelligibility in both Spanish and English. These findings are consistent with diagnosis codes F80.2 (mixed receptive-expressive language disorder) and F80.0 (phonological disorder).

It is important to understand that being raised bilingually is not the cause of Chuy's delays. Children who grow up hearing two languages develop language on a similar overall timeline to children who hear one language, as long as they are getting rich exposure to both, which Chuy clearly is at home. His difficulties appear across both Spanish and English, which tells us this is a true language and speech sound disorder rather than something related to learning two languages at once. His history of prematurity, NICU stay, and chronic ear infections prior to tube placement are all plausible contributing factors, and his strong social engagement, play skills, and nonverbal communication are real strengths that will support his progress in therapy.

Recommendations

1. I recommend that Chuy receive speech-language therapy twice weekly, delivered in a bilingual format that honors both Spanish and English, ideally with a bilingual provider or with consistent interpreter support. Therapy should target expanding his word combinations, increasing his consonant inventory, and reducing reliance on gesture as a sole communication strategy.

2. I recommend that Chuy's current IFSP be updated to reflect these findings. Please ask Mr. Whitfield at the CDSA to schedule a review meeting, and consider adding a new outcome focused specifically on expressive vocabulary growth, noted here as a candidate for IFSP Outcome 3, alongside the existing outcome addressing intelligibility, IFSP Outcome 1.

3. I recommend a structured home-language program such as Hanen's "It Takes Two to Talk," which is well suited to bilingual families and teaches caregivers strategies to expand on Chuy's communication attempts throughout the day, in whichever language feels most natural in the moment.

4. For speech sound work, I recommend a Cycles approach to target his most frequently occurring error patterns, including final consonant deletion and cluster reduction, across both languages in parallel rather than sequentially.

5. I recommend sharing this report with Ms. Lopez at Little Sprouts Daycare so that classroom strategies, such as modeling two-word phrases and allowing extra response time, can be used consistently across settings. It may also help to let Juanito continue being a regular play partner, since Chuy appears motivated to communicate with him.

6. I recommend a repeat hearing screening in six months given Chuy's history of ear infections, even though his most recent results from Dr. Nair were within normal limits.

7. I recommend that Mr. del Río and Ms. Fernández-Ramos continue rich daily exposure to both languages rather than narrowing to one, since this will not slow Chuy's progress and will support his long-term bilingual development.

8. I recommend a re-evaluation in approximately six months to monitor progress and adjust the therapy plan as needed, ideally coordinated with Chuy's next IFSP review.

Next Steps

I will send a copy of this report to Dr. Osei at Blue Ridge Pediatrics at Falls Creek and to Mr. Whitfield at the Western Piedmont CDSA, unless you prefer that I hold off. Our front desk will reach out within the next week to schedule Chuy's first therapy sessions; you can also call us directly at (828) 555-0147 to get started sooner.
